common_name: Pileated Clown Orchid (Venezuela's National Flower, Cinnamon Orchid)

planting.note: Repot only when new roots emerge from the base of a fresh growth in spring, since Catasetum pileatum sheds its leaves and goes fully dormant each winter and resents root disturbance at any other time.

directions: Catasetum pileatum, the national flower of Venezuela, is a deciduous epiphyte that produces thick, ribbed, deciduous pseudobulbs topped with pleated leaves through a warm, humid growing season. Waxy, heavily fragrant flowers in cream, pale yellow, or greenish tones with a broad, deeply cupped lip appear on arching spikes from the base of the mature pseudobulb, and the male flowers carry sensitive trigger antennae that catapult pollen at pollinators when touched. Grow in strong, bright light with heavy watering and regular feeding during active summer growth, then withhold water almost entirely once the leaves drop in fall to mimic its natural dry season. Mount on bark or pot in a very fast-draining bark mix, since standing moisture during winter dormancy quickly rots the resting pseudobulbs.
sources: American Orchid Society — Catasetum culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Catasetum pileatum species profile

planting.note: Divide and repot in spring as new roots appear at the base of a fresh growth; Catasetum expansum drops its leaves and rests dry over winter, so avoid disturbing it once dormancy begins.

directions: Catasetum expansum is a warm-growing Brazilian epiphyte bearing arching sprays of waxy, strongly scented, yellow-green flowers often marked with fine reddish-brown spotting around a broad, helmet-like lip. Like other Catasetum species it is strongly seasonal, pushing new pseudobulbs and leaves during a hot, humid summer growing season and then dropping its foliage entirely for a pronounced winter rest. Water and fertilize generously while new growth is active, then cut back sharply on watering once the leaves yellow and fall, keeping the resting pseudobulbs almost completely dry until new growth resumes in spring. Bright light and a coarse, open bark mix or mounted culture keep the roots healthy through the wet-to-dry cycle.
sources: American Orchid Society — Catasetum culture sheet
Missouri Botanical Garden — Catasetum expansum species profile

planting.note: Repot only in spring when fresh roots emerge from a new growth; Catasetum fimbriatum is deciduous and needs an undisturbed, dry winter rest after its leaves drop.

directions: Native to Brazil, Paraguay, and northern Argentina, Catasetum fimbriatum is one of the more cold-tolerant clown orchids, producing olive-green to yellow-green flowers whose broad lip is edged in a distinctive fine, hair-like fringe. Flower spikes arch from the base of the current season's pseudobulb in mid to late summer, and as with all Catasetum, male-type flowers fire their pollinia forcefully when an insect brushes the sensitive antennae inside the flower. Give it a hot, bright, humid growing season with frequent watering and fertilizing, then a firm, mostly dry rest once the pleated leaves yellow and fall in autumn. Grow in a coarse bark mix or mounted, since the resting pseudobulbs are prone to rot if kept damp through winter.
sources: American Orchid Society — Catasetum culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Catasetum fimbriatum species profile

planting.note: Mount on cork or small slabs, or pot divisions in a fine, well-drained bark-and-moss mix in spring; Pleurothallis grobyi forms dense mats over time and rarely needs repotting more than once every few years.

directions: Pleurothallis grobyi is a widespread, easy-growing miniature epiphyte ranging from Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean into South America, forming dense clumps of short, wiry stems each topped by a single small, fleshy, dark-green leaf. From the base of each leaf, slender arching to pendant spikes carry a succession of tiny, star-shaped flowers in yellow, orange, or reddish tones with delicate, translucent segments, often produced nearly year-round on established plants. Because individual flowers are small, it is grown mounted or in a shallow pan close to eye level where the abundant, jewel-like blooms can be appreciated. It thrives in the same shaded, humid, buoyant-air conditions preferred by many miniature Pleurothallidinae and should never be allowed to dry out completely.
sources: American Orchid Society — Pleurothallis culture notes
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Pleurothallis grobyi species profile

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in spring and pot in a fine, moisture-retentive bark-and-moss mix in a small container or shallow basket; Restrepia elegans prefers steady cool-to-intermediate temperatures and should never fully dry out.

directions: Restrepia elegans is a small, cool-to-intermediate-growing epiphyte from the Andes of Colombia and Venezuela, forming tight tufts of short, wiry stems each bearing a single narrow, leathery leaf. Individual flowers are produced singly and sequentially from the leaf axil over many months, each with narrow, elongated, tail-like sepals fused at the base into a distinctive triangular outline, patterned with fine reddish-brown longitudinal stripes over a pale yellow to cream background. Like its relatives, it flowers almost continuously rather than in one seasonal flush, making it a rewarding miniature for a shaded, humid windowsill or mounted display. Provide constant moisture and buoyant air movement, since these thin-leaved species have little water storage and suffer quickly if allowed to desiccate.
sources: American Orchid Society — Restrepia culture notes
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Restrepia elegans species profile

planting.note: Divide and mount or pot in a fine, humid-holding bark-and-moss mix in spring; Restrepia guttulata is a cool-to-intermediate grower that dislikes drying out or sitting in stagnant, still air.

directions: Restrepia guttulata takes its name from the fine, dot-like spotting — guttulate markings — scattered across the pale ground color of its small, triangular flowers, distinguishing it from the bolder longitudinal striping seen in relatives like Restrepia elegans and Restrepia antennifera. Native to cloud forest habitats in the northern Andes, it forms compact clumps of slender stems, each topped by a single fleshy leaf from whose base individual flowers emerge one at a time over an extended blooming period rather than in a single flush. The narrow, tapering sepals are fused near their base into the characteristic Restrepia triangular shape, with a small, mobile, hinged lip that trembles at the slightest air movement. Keep evenly moist, shaded, and cool, with good humidity and air circulation, mirroring the high-elevation forest conditions where it naturally grows.
sources: American Orchid Society — Restrepia culture notes
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Restrepia guttulata species profile

planting.note: Grow only in an open slatted basket with wide gaps, never a solid pot, since Stanhopea wardii sends its flower spikes straight downward through the drainage medium and cannot bloom if the roots are confined in solid walls.

directions: Stanhopea wardii is a robust epiphyte from Mexico and Central America bearing large, waxy, intensely fragrant flowers in yellow to golden tones, heavily marked with maroon to purplish spots and blotches around the intricately lobed, hinged lip. Like other Stanhopea species, its flower spikes emerge from the base of the pseudobulb and grow straight down, so it must be grown in an open, slatted basket with generous gaps rather than a solid pot, or the buds will be crushed against the container walls before opening. The short-lived flowers, typically open for just two to four days, release a strong, sweet, sometimes cinnamon-like fragrance most intense in the morning. Provide bright, filtered light, ample water and humidity through the growing season, and a brief cooler, slightly drier rest in winter.
sources: American Orchid Society — Stanhopea culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Stanhopea wardii species profile

planting.note: Mount on cork bark or pot in a coarse, fast-draining bark mix in bright, filtered light; Angraecum eburneum forms a large, heavy, long-lived plant, so choose a permanent, well-anchored container or mount from the start.

directions: Angraecum eburneum is a large, robust, monopodial epiphyte native to Madagascar, the Comoros, and nearby Indian Ocean islands, producing a stout, erect stem clothed in broad, leathery, strap-shaped leaves that can eventually reach several feet tall. In fall and winter it sends out arching sprays of large, long-lasting, star-shaped flowers with pale yellow-green sepals and petals surrounding a broad, pure white to ivory lip and a moderate, downward-curving nectar spur. The flowers open with little scent by day but become strongly fragrant at night, attracting moth pollinators in the wild. It tolerates slightly less light and cooler conditions than its famous long-spurred relative Angraecum sesquipedale, making it a somewhat more forgiving choice for a bright but not blazing windowsill or shaded porch.
sources: American Orchid Society — Angraecum culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Angraecum eburneum species profile

planting.note: Mount or pot in a small, well-drained bark basket in spring, and never cut back a spent flower spike, since Psychopsis krameriana continues producing new flowers from the same spike for years.

directions: Psychopsis krameriana is a Central and South American epiphyte closely related to the better-known Psychopsis papilio, sharing the same striking mottled, marbled leaves and tall, wiry, perpetually blooming flower spike. Its flowers are somewhat smaller than papilio's, with narrower, more pointed brown and yellow-barred sepals and petals held above a broad, bright yellow lip, together suggesting the wings and antennae of a butterfly poised in flight. Flower spikes continue to elongate and produce a fresh bloom every few weeks over many years, so the spike should never be cut back after flowering. Grow in bright, filtered light in a small, well-drained basket or mounted on bark, keeping humidity high while allowing the roots to approach dryness between waterings.
sources: American Orchid Society — Psychopsis culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Psychopsis krameriana species profile
